prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock alone, to Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. Having read the chair's questions, I would now argue for it on the physics and the wording of the citation, not on the six-of-eight count, which the chair rightly notes comes partly from members moving after reading each other's ballots (I did so myself, from circuit QED). The distinguishing idea is the magic-wavelength lattice. Choosing the trap wavelength so that the light shift is equal for both clock levels lets one hold thousands of neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, so Doppler and recoil shifts vanish while the many-atom statistical power remains. Neither the frequency comb (2005) nor the single-ion control and Al+ clock (2012) provides that combination. It is a distinct physical mechanism and not an improvement of a recognised tool. The results are also what I look for as a theorist working beside experiments: reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, with the systematics understood in detail. Ye's group then used the same platform as a controlled quantum many-body system, including spin-polarised Fermi gases and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. In answer to the chair's second question, Katori (concept, first strontium lattice clocks) and Ye (accuracy, stability, many-body clock) have separable, documented roles, and all eight members named exactly these two people. I would anchor the citation to the lattice concept and the demonstrated 10^-18 performance, and leave the redefinition of the second and the geodesy and dark-sector applications out of the wording, so that the prize does not depend on events that have not yet happened.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains the one every supporter records. A sceptic will say this is superb metrology adjacent to two earlier prizes, 2005 for the comb and 2012 for ion control and clocks, and that no fundamental-physics result (varying constant, dark-sector signal) has yet come out of the clocks. I think the first part is answered by the mechanism above but not eliminated, since the optical comb is a technical prerequisite, as Olsson says. The second part is simply true, and I accept that the case is a new regime of measurement and not a new law of nature. The credit is also incomplete in a scientific sense: Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde and the Yb and Al+ groups did much of the work that made 10^-18 credible, and the three-name cap forces a choice that I cannot fully resolve from my own expertise. I am a circuit and microwave theorist, not an atomic-clock specialist, so I take priority in the lattice-clock lineage on trust and would welcome an independent expert review of the early lattice-clock proposals before the final vote.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from IceCube to B013 as the clean, mature option, but says he is partly trading discovery value for attribution certainty, and in reply to me said a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 would be hard to defend, with Wallraff missing from the credited names.
responses.response: I accept his points on circuit QED. The Wallraff omission is a real attribution gap in the first strong-coupling experiment, and a second circuit prize right after 2025 is hard to justify, so I have not tried to bring B008 back. His own worry about trading discovery value for clean credit is fair and I share it, but I think it is answered by what the lattice clock opened: tens of times better than microwave standards, tested across laboratories. That is a new regime of measurement, which is a real step beyond refinement. I would also gently note that IceCube remains a candidate for a later year, once the source catalogue firms up beyond a few objects, and I would not want his move to B013 to read as a rejection of it.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the many-atom statistical gain is something ion clocks cannot offer, that the citation must be written around the lattice concept and not around clocks or combs in general, and that a Nobel Prize recognises demonstrated performance, not the metrological decision on the second.
responses.response: I agree on all three, and this is the best answer I have seen to the chair's first question. Ion clocks reach very low systematic uncertainty but with one or few ions, so their stability is limited by quantum projection noise. The lattice reaches comparable accuracy with many atoms, so the averaging time is orders of magnitude shorter, and that is what makes the clock useful for comparisons and for geodesy. I have therefore written my citation around magic-wavelength trapping and the 10^-18 realisation, with no mention of the second or of applications. Where I would push back slightly is on his own wording, 'development of optical lattice clocks', which could be read as a general clock prize. Naming the magic-wavelength concept in the citation does more to separate it from 2005 and 2012.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B048 first as a new state of matter with a symmetry-based invariant, accepts that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 3D topological insulator work make attribution fragile, and asks whether I see the BHZ omission as disqualifying.
responses.response: I do not think the BHZ omission is disqualifying on science, but I do think it is disqualifying for a three-name prize this year, which I believe he concedes. The HgTe experiment was motivated by the BHZ prediction, and with Zhang deceased, the committee would be crediting Molenkamp's measurement without the theory that told him where to look. The 3D work in the same framework cannot be covered by the cap either, and the 2016 prize leaves the marginal novelty to be explained. I would rank B048 as a serious alternative, which is why it stays in my list, but I would not try to fix its credit in committee. I also agree with his comparison to B008: neither of us can honestly say that our own preferred field has a clean three-name credit this year, which is an argument for the clock.

responses.point: Olsson notes that an optical comb is a necessary technical foundation for any optical clock, so the committee must be sure the lattice-clock contribution is distinct, and that she recalls priority from memory and not from documents. She also disclosed my Chalmers connection.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure, and I accept the comb point as a technical fact: the comb is how optical frequencies are counted. But the same is true of the laser and the vacuum chamber, and the question for the prize is what was new. The new thing was the trapping scheme, which has no counterpart in the comb prize. I share her memory-based caveat about priority, and I think we should say openly in the final record that neither of us is verifying the early lattice-clock history from documents. I would also note, as she does, that B050 is her own field, which is why her move away from it to B013 carries weight with me.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B034 as the conceptual root of the geometric-phase programmes but states that it is the weakest on opening support and that priority (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam, Mead-Truhlar, Simon) and the death of Bohm are obstacles, naming B013 and B048 as fallbacks.
responses.response: I agree with him that the Aharonov-Bohm and Berry ideas are a deep root, and that several shortlisted topics are downstream of them. But the strength of his own list of obstacles is what keeps me from supporting it as a prize in this round: the credit cannot be written down without choosing among at least five contributors. A prize for a unifying concept needs a name set that the community already accepts. I note that he already names B013 as his fallback, and I would like to hear whether the clock mechanism is, in his terms, a clear mechanism and a clear first identifier. I think it is, with Katori as the first identifier of the magic-wavelength condition.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a mechanism-based argument (magic-wavelength trapping with many atoms) as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or will read the lattice clock as the third prize in one metrology lineage.

Whether Katori and Ye are enough: the hands-on contributions of Ludlow, Lemke, Hinkley, Bloom, Takamoto, Lemonde and the Yb and Al+ groups cannot be assessed from my expertise, and I would welcome an independent expert review of the earliest lattice-clock proposals.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second, or a first fundamental-physics result from the clocks, should change the timing; I lean towards not waiting, but I hold this loosely.
I judge astrophysical, topological-materials and electron-optics candidates at much less depth than quantum optics and circuits, and my views on B035, B048 and B050 rely on colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and circuit QED (WACQT colleagues include Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson). That is a real connection to B008, which I ranked first in my opening, and I have withdrawn it from my configuration and would recuse myself from any decision centred on B008. I also disclose, as Kroll and Olsson noted, my Chalmers affiliation and my proximity to Kroll through WACQT and to Olsson and Mehlig through the Gothenburg environment. None of this touches B013, Katori or Ye, with whom I have no known personal, collaborative or institutional link.
